title: Self-Employment and Small Business
summary: Self-employment is an economic activity which a person performs on their own as a gainful occupation; it may consist of producing and selling goods, buying and selling goods or rendering services for a price, taking the risk of mobilising inputs. Wage (paid) employment is work for a wage or salary under an employer. Characteristics: doing something on one's own for a livelihood; ownership and management by the person (possibly with one or two helpers); earnings are not fixed; the owner bears the profit and the risk of loss (direct link between effort and reward); requires some capital; freedom of decision; freedom to work within legal regulations.

Importance: advantages of small business (easy to start, little capital, avoids evils of large-scale business such as pollution and exploitation); preferred over wage employment (no limit on earnings, quick decisions); develops the spirit of entrepreneurship (a launching pad); promotes individualised services (tailoring, repairs); scope for creativity (handicrafts, handloom); reduces unemployment; boon to those who cannot pursue higher education.

Avenues of self-employment: trading (grocery or stationery shop, wholesale, agency, stockist, real estate); manufacturing (bricks, bakery and confectionery, farming, dairy, poultry, sericulture, fisheries); professionals (lawyers, doctors, chartered accountants, architects, journalists, who follow a code of conduct); individualised services (tailoring, motor repair, hair cutting, fashion designing, interior decoration).

A small business is actively managed by its owners, operates in a local area and is relatively small in size. Under the MSMED Act 2006 (investment in plant and machinery, excluding land and building): manufacturing micro up to Rs 25 lakh, small Rs 25 lakh to Rs 5 crore; service micro up to Rs 10 lakh, small Rs 10 lakh to Rs 2 crore. Characteristics: owned and managed by one or a few persons; owners take part in day-to-day work, so quick decisions; limited area of operation; labour intensive and need less capital; use local resources and are located near raw materials and labour; short gestation period; flexible operation.

Types: small-scale enterprises; micro enterprises; ancillary industrial undertakings (supply not less than 50 per cent of production to another industry); village industries (in rural areas, with or without power); cottage industries (simple products using art or skill, mainly with family members, such as handicrafts and filigree, not defined by capital); and trading units (small retailers).

Importance in India: small industries account for about 95 per cent of industrial units, 35 per cent of manufacturing output, 80 per cent of industrial employment and about 45 per cent of exports. They generate employment quickly, need less capital, cost less to produce by using local resources, mobilise untapped resources, promote balanced regional development, improve the national image through exports and raise the standard of living. Scope: trading, personalised services, self-employment, products with limited demand, ancillary units for large industries, BPO and businesses needing constant interaction with customers.

Government policy: liberalised credit; items reserved for small industries; GST exemption and composition scheme; SIDBI, NABARD, DICs; Ministry of MSME; capital subsidy; grant for ISO 9000 certification; Deendayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana; concessional land, power and water; incentives for rural and backward areas; industrial estates; the MUDRA scheme (capital to small businesses); Skill India Mission; Stand-up India (2015: credit for women, SC and ST entrepreneurs to set up new enterprises). Institutions: NSIC (1955; machinery on hire purchase and lease, export marketing, technology upgradation); State Small Industries Development Corporations (raw materials, machinery on hire purchase, marketing); NABARD (1982; rural finance for small, cottage and village industries); SIDBI (1990; apex bank for financing small industries); Small Industries Service Institutions (consultancy, training, technical support, entrepreneurship programmes, trade information); District Industries Centres (industrial potential surveys, implementation of schemes, appraising proposals, guidance on machinery and raw materials).

objective: Which business is considered a 'Small Business'? Explain.

A business actively managed by its owners, operating in a local area and small in size; under MSMED Act 2006 manufacturing units with plant and machinery investment up to Rs 5 crore (services up to Rs 2 crore) are small enterprises.
Name any two avenues of self-employment.
Trading and manufacturing (also professionals and individualised services).
A person running a grocery shop and a person running a tailoring shop.
Identify the avenue of self-employment: (a) a farmer with four acres, (b) a doctor running a clinic, (c) Hari repairs gold chains.
Expand: (i) DIC (ii) SIDBI (iii) NABARD (iv) NSIC (v) SSIDC.

(i) District Industries Centre. (ii) Small Industries Development Bank of India. (iii) National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development. (iv) National Small Industries Corporation. (v) State Small Industries Development Corporation.

vsa: How does small business help in 'Balanced Regional Development'?
Small units can be set up near the sources of local resources in backward and rural areas, spreading industry and employment evenly across regions.
April 2026
Explain why 'local resources' are preferred by small units.
They are cheaper and easily available, cut transport cost and keep the cost of production low.
April 2026
Describe the role of SIDBI and SISI in supporting small business in India.
SIDBI is the apex institution financing and developing small industries; SISIs give consultancy, training and technical and market information.
October 2024
Describe the role of NSIC and NABARD in supporting small business.
NSIC supplies machinery on hire purchase or lease and helps in marketing; NABARD provides finance for rural small, cottage and village industries.
October 2024
Define self-employment.
An economic activity performed by a person on their own as a gainful occupation, bearing the risk and taking the profit.
October 2025
State any two qualities required for self-employment.
Willingness to take risk and hard work (also decision-making ability).
April 2025
What is a micro enterprise?
A unit whose investment in plant and machinery is up to Rs 25 lakh (manufacturing) or Rs 10 lakh (services).
State any two characteristics of small business.
Owned and managed by one or a few persons and limited area of operation.
sa: Mention any four characteristics of self-employment.
Doing work on one's own, uncertain earnings, owner bears risk and takes profit and freedom of decision.
Explain any two avenues of self-employment.
Trading (shops, wholesale, agency) and individualised services (tailoring, repair, hair cutting).
State any three characteristics of small business.
Owner-managed, limited area of operation, uses local resources and flexible.
Explain any three types of small business.
Micro enterprises, ancillary units supplying at least 50 per cent to another industry and cottage industries run by family members.
Explain any three ways in which the government supports small business.
Liberal credit, reserved items and industrial estates, subsidies, MUDRA loans and Skill India.
Explain the role of District Industries Centres.
They survey industrial potential, implement schemes, appraise proposals and guide on machinery and raw materials.
la: Explain the importance of self-employment in an economy.
It offsets unemployment, is a better alternative to wage employment, develops entrepreneurship, offers individualised services and creativity, and benefits those who cannot continue higher education.
Explain any five forms in which small business can operate in India.
Small-scale enterprises, micro enterprises, ancillary undertakings, village industries, cottage industries and trading units.
Explain the importance of small business in India.
It generates employment, needs less capital, reduces cost through local resources, mobilises resources, aids regional development, exports and living standards.
Explain the government support and institutions for small business.
Credit, subsidies, reservation, MUDRA and Stand-up India, NSIC, SIDBI, NABARD, SISI and DIC.
